newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 gains 11.6 percent in 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 gains 11.6 percent in 1996.

text.p: Britain's FTSE 100 index of blue-chip stocks set the latest of a series of record highs on Tuesday, although its performance through the year remained well below its strongest since it was created in January 1984.

The FTSE closed 2.8 points higher on the day at 4,118.5, its fifth record close of the past month, after a truncated New Year's Eve trading session which left it around 11.6 percent higher than it ended last year.
Compared with a 20.3 percent rise in 1995 and a 35 percent advance in 1989 -- its biggest annual gain -- the FTSE's showing was pedestrian.

However, the index still managed to beat the expectations of most investment strategists -- only the most optimistic had forecast a year-end 4,100 -- while in dollar terms it nearly matched the rip-roaring gains on Wall Street.
It was also a more comforting performance than the 10 percent decline in 1994 and the 12 percent drop in 1990, the only two years in which it has recorded an annual decline.
Strategists said 1996 had been a "year of two halves" for the British equity market, with a cautious first six months eventually giving way to a more upbeat, though volatile, second half of the year.

Until the end of July the FTSE 100 was struggling to make progress against a background of political uncertainties and sluggish profit prospects. But it came to life in the second half of the year as Wall Street romped to a series of new peaks.

"We started the year dogged by the idea of profit downgradings and worries over politics and those constrained things very much in the first half," said Phillip Isherwood, strategist at Kleinwort Benson.
"In the second half we found we could rally with Wall Street."

Strategist Corey Miller at Credit Lyonnais Laing said the strong profitability of British companies had fuelled a boom in takeovers, share buybacks and special dividends that had injected cash into the market.
"Really it has all been about cash," said Miller.
"The cash-generative quality of the corporate sector has been so strong, it has been responsible for pushing the market to all-time highs and it is going to continue next year.
"Interest rates are going to go up in the first half of next year but not enough to choke off the liquidity."
Strategists polled by Reuters earlier this month expected the FTSE 100 to end 1997 at between 4,000 and 4,500 -- with an average of 4,251, or 3.2 percent above its 1996 close.

The outlook for next year remains clouded by uncertainties over the forthcoming British election that must be held by the end of May, coupled with fears that strengthening economic growth might lead to higher inflation.
There are also significant worries that Wall Street might experience a long-awaited correction, while persistent strength in sterling will also squeeze the profits of major exporters.
Yet despite the cloudy prospects for next year, some market pundits believe London could outperform other leading international equity markets, having underperformed during 1996.

"There are risks out there to do with the election and the strength of the currency," said Miller, "but as long as cash flow is very strong, that should help protect the market from those risks and uncertainties."

Market experts say the prospective dividend yield of more than four percent makes the British market look relatively good value compared with other world markets, and that the risks associated with a Labour government should already have been discounted.
"In 1996 a lot of the bears have clearly been frustrated," said Isherwood at Kleinwort. "But most of the downside risks are in the market already."
